newsitem.title: USA: Hepatitis inoculations continue in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Hepatitis inoculations continue in Michigan.

text.p: Thousands of Michigan school children were inoculated against the hepatitis A virus on Thursday as health departments tracked down people who ate contaminated frozen strawberry desserts.

The tainted desserts were distributed to schools in 28 Michigan counties as part of the federal school lunch program. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control said on Wednesday the only confirmed cases of people made sick by the nationally distributed berries were 153 schoolchildren and parents in Michigan.

Michigan officials cautioned the full extent of the problem may not be known for a few more weeks since the berries were still being consumed late last week. Hepatitis A takes between two and six weeks to develop.

In Kent County in western Michigan, health department workers on Thursday visited the final eight schools where the berries were served in the last two weeks, said Mike Mullet, community relations coordinator for the county's health department in Grand Rapids.

Mullet said the shots are being given to about 2,200 children at three high schools, two middle schools and three elementary schools in Kent County. But students at dozens of schools in the county were served the berries since early December, when they were first shipped to Michigan.
"It's not inaccurate to say the majority of schools served them," he said, referring to Kent County.

Dennis Bandy, Special Olympics coordinator for Southgate, Mich., said that about 30 people on his teams ate the berries at a Special Olympics event in Grand Rapids on March 22 attended by about 1,400 people.
"The kids are taking it pretty good. Nobody panicked," Bandy said of the inoculation program "As long as the adults don't panic, the kids aren't going to panic."

An immune globulin, which is not a vaccine, contains antibodies to help prevent the illness. However, it is only effective for 14 days from the time the illness was contracted, meaning people who ate the berries weeks ago would not be helped.
Many of the berries were served during Valentine's Day, meaning any new cases should be showing up shortly, said Mullet.
A spokeswoman for the Michigan State Department of Community Health said the agency will issue an update later on Thursday.
